title: How does Adam Tooze think about American history?
gist: Video page for Adam Tooze on how he thinks about American history; the captured text contains no transcript, only headline-level related FP content centered on the US-Iran peace deal (Hormuz ambiguity, follow-through risk) and US power and soft-power erosion.

insights.claim: Foreign Policy's related coverage presents competing views on the US-Iran peace deal: Ravi Agrawal argues the deal will hold, while Daniel Byman argues it sets the stage for more conflict because Trump is better at fanfare than follow-up.
insights.so_what: Divergent expert views on deal durability imply continued geopolitical risk premium in oil.
insights.quote: As his Gaza agreement has shown, Trump is better at fanfare than follow-up.
insights.locator: How the Iran Deal Sets the Stage for More Conflict
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze

insights.claim: Related FP analysis by Keith Johnson flags that the US-Iran deal is hazy on the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.so_what: Ambiguity on Hormuz transit leaves tail risk for global oil and LNG shipping.
insights.quote: The Iran Deal Is Hazy on Hormuz
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze

insights.claim: Adam Tooze, director of the European Institute at Columbia University, discusses his framework for thinking about American history in a Foreign Policy video; the page itself carries no transcript, while surrounding pieces argue US power is 'wrung out' and America's soft power has ended.
insights.so_what: A recurring elite narrative of US decline and overstretch supports hedging and diversification-away-from-US themes.
insights.locator: How does Adam Tooze think about American history?
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
